To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the frequency of GAG-specific CD8+ and CD4+ T cells in the blood of HIV-infected infants correlates with the level of HIV in the blood, and that infants with more GAG-specific T cells have a lower viral load and are less likely to progress to AIDS.
HIV-specific gag responses in HIV-infant correlate with clinical outcome, inversely with viral loads and that these responses correlate with survival.
HIV-specific T cell frequencies correlate with survival and inversely with HIV viral load in the first year after birth.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the immune correlates of protection from HIV infection.
understanding the immune correlates of HIV disease progression and the development of a vaccine that will prevent disease in infants.
the development of a vaccine that will protect HIV-exposed infants from infection and disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the early presence (3 months of age) of quantitatively high HIV gag-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cell responses in infants is associated with decreased viral load and decreased mortality in HIV-infected children.
HIV-specific T cell immune response in early infancy is associated with clinical outcome and viral load in HIV-exposed infants.
the presence of Gag-specific T cells in the early stages of life is a predictor of survival in HIV-infected children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HIV-specific T cell response in early infancy correlate inversely with viral loads and positively with clinical outcome.
HIV-specific Gag responses in the first 3-6 months of life correlate inversely with viremia and mortality in HIV-infected African infants.
the early presence (3 months) of quantitatively greater Gag-specific T cells in HIV-infected African infants is associated with decreased mortality in the following 12 months.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the presence of a robust T cell response against Gag in HIV infected infants in the first year is associated with lower viremia and improved survival in the first year, suggesting a protective role for Gag-specific T cells in the first year.
early Gag-specific T cells correlate with better clinical outcomes in HIV-infected children.
early HIV-specific T cell immunity is important in controlling HIV infection in infants and is associated with improved survival in the first year.
